title: Sufi saints of India
hook: Mu'in al-Din Chishti in Ajmer and Nizam al-Din in Delhi, whose shrines draw people of all faiths

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ulugh Beg, who built an observatory and read the stars as signs. Your line was the astronomer king.

Thursday evening in Delhi. A narrow lane, so packed you move with the crowd, past stalls selling rose petals, sheets of embroidered cloth, sweets and prayer caps. At the end, a courtyard of white marble and a tomb under a dome. Men and women in head coverings sit on the floor. Some are Muslims. Some are Hindus, some Sikhs, some Christians, some just curious. Then the singers start: a harmonium, hand drums, voices rising and falling in poems about longing for God. This is the shrine of a Sufi saint who died long ago, and people still gather around his grave. Today: Sufi saints of India.
screen: `A PACKED LANE OF ROSE PETALS.` → `A MARBLE COURTYARD AND A TOMB.` → `PEOPLE OF EVERY FAITH, SINGING.`

segments.voice: Two names lead the way. Mu'in al-Din Chishti came to India from the lands to the west and settled in Ajmer, in Rajasthan. Nizam al-Din Awliya taught later in Delhi, in the same Sufi line, the Chishti order. Both are remembered not for armies or palaces but for open doors. Tradition says Nizam al-Din's lodge fed visitors all day long, rich or poor, Muslim or not, and that he gave away what came to him rather than keep it. At Ajmer today, huge cooking pots are filled and the food is served to whoever comes. Pilgrims call Mu'in al-Din Gharib Nawaz, the friend of the poor. Why food? The Qur'an praises those who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner for love of God. In Pickthall's translation, they say: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Nizam al-Din's student was the poet Amir Khusrau, remembered for songs still sung at these shrines, and he is buried near his teacher. The singing in that Delhi courtyard, qawwali, is linked to that circle. Muslims do not all see these shrines the same way. Some treasure the visit, the music and the blessing of a holy person's memory. Others, pointing to the Prophet's teaching that prayer belongs to God alone, avoid praying at graves and question the music. Both are Muslims, reading the same sources. At the shrines, the pots are still full. The open kitchen.
screen: `AJMER AND DELHI.` · `THE FRIEND OF THE POOR.` · `WE FEED YOU FOR THE SAKE OF ALLAH.` · `MUSLIMS SEE SHRINES DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `THE OPEN KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Think about the next meal you'll share or make, and who might be fed who isn't usually at your table: a neighbor living alone, a coworker who eats at their desk, a friend in a hard week. Picture handing them a plate and wanting nothing back, not even thanks. If you pray, you can ask that the food be a blessing.
Chishti. The Sufi order of teachers like Mu'in al-Din in Ajmer and Nizam al-Din in Delhi, whose shrines feed and welcome people of every faith. Today's word.
Your line: the open kitchen. Food for whoever comes, wanting nothing back. That's day nine hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: At Sufi shrines (dargahs) in South Asia, visitors offer flowers and cloth, listen to qawwali, and receive food cooked in large pots and served to all, while other Muslims, citing the teaching that prayer belongs to God alone, avoid shrine customs.
